claim: Acute kidney injury (AKI) afflicts 1.2 million hospitalized patients annually in the US.
source: Acute kidney injury (AKI) afflicts 1.2 million hospitalized patients annually in the US; 20–50% of AKI survivors progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD), increasing their risk for dialysis-dependency, cardiovascular events, and mortality (Chawla et al., 2014; Lewington et al., 2013; Strausser et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chawla et al., 2014; Lewington et al., 2013; Strausser et al., 2018).

claim: 20–50% of AKI survivors progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD).
source: Acute kidney injury (AKI) afflicts 1.2 million hospitalized patients annually in the US; 20–50% of AKI survivors progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD), increasing their risk for dialysis-dependency, cardiovascular events, and mortality (Chawla et al., 2014; Lewington et al., 2013; Strausser et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chawla et al., 2014; Lewington et al., 2013; Strausser et al., 2018).

claim: AKI survivors who progress to CKD have increased risk for dialysis-dependency, cardiovascular events, and mortality.
source: Acute kidney injury (AKI) afflicts 1.2 million hospitalized patients annually in the US; 20–50% of AKI survivors progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD), increasing their risk for dialysis-dependency, cardiovascular events, and mortality (Chawla et al., 2014; Lewington et al., 2013; Strausser et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chawla et al., 2014; Lewington et al., 2013; Strausser et al., 2018).

claim: There are no targeted therapies to treat AKI or to prevent AKI to CKD transition other than general supportive care.
source: Other than general supportive care, there are no targeted therapies to treat AKI or to prevent AKI to CKD transition.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of medical knowledge and practice, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Damage to proximal tubular (PT) epithelial cells after severe AKI is a critical mechanism driving transition to CKD.
source: Clinical and preclinical studies have identified damage to proximal tubular (PT) epithelial cells after severe AKI as a critical mechanism driving transition to CKD (Strausser et al., 2018; Chawla et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Cippà et al., 2018; Ferenbach and Bonventre, 2015; Humphreys, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple clinical and preclinical studies (Strausser et al., 2018; Chawla et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Cippà et al., 2018; Ferenbach and Bonventre, 2015; Humphreys, 2018).

claim: PT cells are most severely affected by acute ischemic and toxic injuries due to their high metabolic and energy-intensive transporter activities.
source: PT cells are most severely affected by acute ischemic and toxic injuries due to their high metabolic and energy-intensive transporter activities required to maintain normal homeostasis of body fluids (Ferenbach and Bonventre, 2015; Humphreys, 2018; Gewin, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ferenbach and Bonventre, 2015; Humphreys, 2018; Gewin, 2018).

claim: Damaged PT cells adopt heterogeneous molecular states during the renal repair process.
source: In the renal repair process, damaged PT cells adopt heterogeneous molecular states (Kirita et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Kirita et al., 2020).

claim: Damaged PT cells reactivate genes normally active during renal development.
source: They reactivate genes normally active during renal development (Rudman-Melnick et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2015), alter their dependency on metabolic fuels (Legouis et al., 2020), change their morphology, and proliferate to replenish the areas of denuded epithelium in the proximal tubule (Ferenbach and Bonventre, 2015; Witzgall et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Rudman-Melnick et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2015).

claim: Damaged PT cells alter their dependency on metabolic fuels during repair.
source: They reactivate genes normally active during renal development (Rudman-Melnick et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2015), alter their dependency on metabolic fuels (Legouis et al., 2020), change their morphology, and proliferate to replenish the areas of denuded epithelium in the proximal tubule (Ferenbach and Bonventre, 2015; Witzgall et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Legouis et al., 2020).

claim: Damaged PT cells change their morphology and proliferate to replenish areas of denuded epithelium in the proximal tubule.
source: They reactivate genes normally active during renal development (Rudman-Melnick et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2015), alter their dependency on metabolic fuels (Legouis et al., 2020), change their morphology, and proliferate to replenish the areas of denuded epithelium in the proximal tubule (Ferenbach and Bonventre, 2015; Witzgall et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ferenbach and Bonventre, 2015; Witzgall et al., 1994).

claim: After mild kidney damage, PT cells return to their original state by redifferentiation, with resolution of inflammation and fibrosis.
source: When the initial damage to kidneys is mild, PT cells subsequently return to their original state by redifferentiation, with resolution of inflammation and fibrosis (Ferenbach and Bonventre, 2015; Kirita et al., 2020; Rudman-Melnick et al., 2020; Legouis et al., 2020; Witzgall et al., 1994; Berger et al., 2014; Kusaba et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ferenbach and Bonventre, 2015; Kirita et al., 2020; Rudman-Melnick et al., 2020; Legouis et al., 2020; Witzgall et al., 1994; Berger et al., 2014; Kusaba et al., 2014).

claim: After extensive, prolonged, or recurrent damage, damaged PT cells fail to redifferentiate, leading to persistent inflammation, fibrosis, and eventual cell death.
source: However, if damage is more extensive, prolonged, or recurrent, the damaged cells fail to redifferentiate, leading to persistent inflammation, fibrosis, and eventual cell death.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field, inferred from the context of the preceding sentence about mild injury outcomes.

claim: Ferroptosis is a distinct non-apoptotic form of regulated cell death.
source: One of the critical pathways involved in AKI pathogenesis and proximal tubular cell death is ferroptosis, a distinct non-apoptotic form of regulated cell death (Stockwell et al., 2017; Dixon et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2014; Kagan et al., 2017; Doll et al., 2017; Alim et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020; Linkermann et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Stockwell et al., 2017; Dixon et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2014; Kagan et al., 2017; Doll et al., 2017; Alim et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020; Linkermann et al., 2014).

claim: Ferroptosis is a critical pathway involved in AKI pathogenesis and proximal tubular cell death.
source: One of the critical pathways involved in AKI pathogenesis and proximal tubular cell death is ferroptosis, a distinct non-apoptotic form of regulated cell death (Stockwell et al., 2017; Dixon et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2014; Kagan et al., 2017; Doll et al., 2017; Alim et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020; Linkermann et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Stockwell et al., 2017; Dixon et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2014; Kagan et al., 2017; Doll et al., 2017; Alim et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020; Linkermann et al., 2014).

claim: An imbalance between the generation of lipid peroxides and their detoxification induces overwhelming accumulation of lipid peroxides (ferroptotic stress), triggering ferroptosis.
source: An imbalance between the generation of lipid peroxides and their detoxification induces overwhelming accumulation of lipid peroxides (ferroptotic stress), triggering ferroptosis (Stockwell et al., 2017; Alim et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Stockwell et al., 2017; Alim et al., 2019).

claim: The glutathione/glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) axis is the central defense pathway to prevent ferroptotic stress and ferroptosis.
source: The glutathione/glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) axis is the central defense pathway to prevent ferroptotic stress and ferroptosis (Stockwell et al., 2017; Dixon et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2014; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Stockwell et al., 2017; Dixon et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2014; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014).

claim: Global genetic deletion of Gpx4 in mice causes renal tubular epithelial death and acute kidney injury.
source: Global genetic deletion of Gpx4 in mice causes renal tubular epithelial death and acute kidney injury, identifying renal tubular epithelial cells as one of the cell types most vulnerable to ferroptotic stress (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014).

claim: Renal tubular epithelial cells are one of the cell types most vulnerable to ferroptotic stress.
source: Global genetic deletion of Gpx4 in mice causes renal tubular epithelial death and acute kidney injury, identifying renal tubular epithelial cells as one of the cell types most vulnerable to ferroptotic stress (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014) and is inferred from the experimental result of Gpx4 deletion.

claim: Reduced glutathione and NADPH availability render ischemia-reperfusion injured kidneys vulnerable to ferroptotic stress.
source: Moreover, reduced glutathione and NADPH availability further render ischemia-reperfusion injured kidneys vulnerable to ferroptotic stress (Strausser et al., 2018; Nezu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Strausser et al., 2018; Nezu et al., 2017).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of ferroptotic cell death ameliorates AKI severity.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that pharmacological inhibition of ferroptotic cell death ameliorates AKI severity and excess ferroptotic stress has been linked to failed renal repair in patients, suggesting a new therapeutic target (Zhao et al., 2020; Linkermann et al., 2014; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Wenzel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Zhao et al., 2020; Linkermann et al., 2014; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Wenzel et al., 2017).

claim: Excess ferroptotic stress has been linked to failed renal repair in patients.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that pharmacological inhibition of ferroptotic cell death ameliorates AKI severity and excess ferroptotic stress has been linked to failed renal repair in patients, suggesting a new therapeutic target (Zhao et al., 2020; Linkermann et al., 2014; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Wenzel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Zhao et al., 2020; Linkermann et al., 2014; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Wenzel et al., 2017).

claim: Molecular regulators of necroptosis contribute to disease pathogenesis by pathways independent of their roles in triggering cell death.
source: Interestingly, recent evidence suggests that molecular regulators of necroptosis, another form of regulated cell death, contribute to disease pathogenesis by additional pathways independent of their well-documented roles in triggering cell death (Daniels et al., 2017; Moriwaki and Chan, 2016; Moriwaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Daniels et al., 2017; Moriwaki and Chan, 2016; Moriwaki et al., 2014).

claim: The study identifies a molecularly distinct, damage-associated PT cell state that is dynamically and differentially regulated during successful versus failed repair.
source: Here, using complementary single-cell transcriptomic and mouse genetic approaches, we identify the role of a molecularly distinct, damage-associated, PT cell state that is dynamically and differentially regulated during successful versus failed repair.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the single-cell transcriptomic data and mouse genetic experiments described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ferroptotic stress in PT cells enhances the damage-associated state, in addition to triggering cell death.
source: Furthermore, we provide mechanistic evidence that ferroptotic stress in PT cells enhances this damage-associated state, in addition to triggering cell death, thereby promoting failed renal repair and the AKI-to-CKD transition.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the genetic deletion experiments of Gpx4 and pharmacological inhibition studies described in the manuscript.

claim: Extending renal ischemic times from 20 min to 30 min distinguishes successful from failed renal repair in mouse models.
source: To identify cellular mechanisms that promote maladaptive repair after severe kidney injury, we first developed and optimized mouse models for 'successful' versus 'failed' renal repair after ischemia-reperfusion-induced injury (IRI). This was achieved by extending renal ischemic times from 20 min for successful recovery to 30 min for failed recovery (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse models described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: After mild injury (20 min ischemia), inflammation and macrophage accumulation resolved within 21 days.
source: After mild injury, histologic examination showed that inflammation and macrophage accumulation resolved within 21 days (ischemic time 20 min; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by histologic examination data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, D and E.

claim: After severe injury (30 min ischemia), there was progressive epithelial damage and fibrosis, and the accumulation of F4/80+ macrophages persisted for at least 6 months.
source: By contrast, after severe injury there was progressive epithelial damage and fibrosis, and the accumulation of F4/80+ macrophages persisted around the damaged epithelial cells for at least 6 months (ischemic time 30 min; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, D and E; and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by histologic examination data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, D and E; and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: High-quality transcriptome data from a total of 18,258 cells from injured kidneys (IRI) and homeostatic uninjured kidneys (Homeo) were obtained.
source: High-quality transcriptome data from a total of 18,258 cells from injured kidneys (IRI) and homeostatic uninjured kidneys (Homeo) were obtained (Figure 1, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell RNA sequencing data described in the methods and shown in Figure 1, B and C.

claim: Unsupervised clustering analysis resolved 21 separate clusters, representing distinct cell types.
source: Using a Seurat integration algorithm that normalizes data and removes potential batch effects (Stuart et al., 2019; Hafemeister and Satija, 2019), we integrated the transcriptome data from each condition and performed unsupervised clustering analysis of the integrated dataset. Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) resolved 21 separate clusters, representing distinct cell types (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Known cell-type-specific damage-induced genes such as Havcr1, Krt8, Krt20, and Lcn2 were successfully identified selectively in ischemia-reperfusion-injured (IRI) kidneys, but not in homeostatic uninjured control kidneys.
source: We successfully identified known cell-type-specific damage-induced genes such as Havcr1 (kidney injury molecule-1, KIM1), Krt8 (keratin 8), Krt20 (keratin 20), and Lcn2 (neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin, NGAL) selectively in ischemia-reperfusion-injured (IRI) kidneys, but not in homeostatic uninjured control kidneys (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), (Liu et al., 2017; Ichimura et al., 2008; Paragas et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and citations to published literature (Liu et al., 2017; Ichimura et al., 2008; Paragas et al., 2011).

claim: Damage-associated tubular epithelial clusters (DA-PT, DA-TAL, and DA-DCT) had lost or reduced expression of 'normal' mature epithelial cell marker genes but highly expressed damage-induced genes.
source: However, we also identified additional damage-associated tubular epithelial clusters (Figure 1C, arrowheads; DA-PT, DA-TAL, and DA-DCT) that had lost or reduced expression of 'normal' mature epithelial cell marker genes but highly expressed damage-induced genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, B and C, Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1C, arrowheads; and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, B and C.

claim: A damage-associated proximal tubular cell state (DA-PT cluster) shows reduced homeostatic gene expression and enrichment for genes associated with both renal development and kidney injury in human and mouse.
source: Among these damage-associated epithelial cell clusters, we found a damage-associated proximal tubular cell state (See DA-PT cluster), which shows reduced homeostatic gene expression (ex. Lrp2, Slc34a1, Hnf4a, and Acsm2) and enrichment for genes associated with both renal development and kidney injury in human and mouse (ex. Cdh6, Sox9, Sox4, Cited2, Vcam1, Vim, and Havcr1; Figure 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5B and Figure 1—figure supplement 6A), (Combes et al., 2019a; Famulski et al., 2012; Adam et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 6A, and citations to published literature (Combes et al., 2019a; Famulski et al., 2012; Adam et al., 2017).

claim: Gene ontology enrichment analyses of the DA-PT cellular population revealed proinflammatory molecular signatures and enriched expression of chemokines and cytokines such as Cxcl2, Cxcl1, Ccl2, and Spp1.
source: Moreover, gene ontology enrichment analyses of this cellular population revealed proinflammatory molecular signatures and enriched expression of chemokines and cytokines such as Cxcl2, Cxcl1, Ccl2, and Spp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B,D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, D and E.

claim: Reduced expression of Hnf4a and upregulation of Cdh6 suggest that the cells in the DA-PT cluster are in a less differentiated cell state.
source: Reduced expression of Hnf4a, which is a transcription factor essential for the maturation of PT cells (Marable et al., 2018; Marable et al., 2020), and other homeostatic genes and upregulation of Cdh6, which is selectively expressed in immature proximal tubule progenitors in development and is essential for renal epithelialization (Marable et al., 2020; Cho et al., 1998; Mah et al., 2000), suggest that the cells in this cluster (DA-PT) are in a less differentiated cell state (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 6A), (Marable et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 6A, and citations to published literature (Marable et al., 2018; Marable et al., 2020; Cho et al., 1998; Mah et al., 2000).

claim: The top 100 genes enriched in immature early PT cells in neonatal kidneys were mainly expressed in the damage-associated PT cell state (DA-PT).
source: Then, we compared the transcriptional signature of this damage-associated PT cell state with previously published neonatal kidney single-cell RNA seq data (GSE94333, Figure 1—figure supplement 7, A and B), (Adam et al., 2017). The top 100 genes enriched in immature early PT cells in neonatal kidneys were mainly expressed in this damage-associated PT cell state (DA-PT, Figure 1—figure supplement 7, C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7, C and D, and citation to published data (Adam et al., 2017).

claim: SOX9 nuclear accumulation was observed in VCAM1+ proximal tubular cells in kidneys with failed repair.
source: To validate this finding, we performed immunofluorescence for SOX9 and VCAM1 in histological sections of kidneys with failed repair. SOX9 nuclear accumulation was observed in VCAM1+ proximal tubular cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Pseudotime trajectory analysis predicted a differentiation trajectory originating from PT to DA-PT.
source: To understand the lineage hierarchy of PT cell states, we analyzed PT cells from differentiated and damage-associated PT cell clusters (PT and DA-PT in Figure 1B) using two algorithm tools (Monocle 3 and Velocyto) that allow the computational prediction of cell differentiation trajectories (Cao et al., 2019; La Manno et al., 2018). By placing each cell from the entire dataset in pseudotime we observed a predicted differentiation trajectory originating from PT to DA-PT (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 8, A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 8, A and B.

claim: RNA velocity analysis showed two trajectories running in opposite directions: one toward the area with high levels of damage-induced genes (dedifferentiation path) and the other toward the area with high levels of maturation-associated genes (redifferentiation path).
source: We then performed RNA velocity analysis, which predicts the cell state trajectory based on the ratio between unspliced and spliced mRNA expressions, for these two PT cell states from the post-IRI dataset on day 7. Our RNA velocity analysis showed two trajectories running in opposite directions from the middle of the cluster, a position where genes associated with tubular maturation and damage are both not highly expressed (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 8C). One projects toward the area with high levels of damage-induced genes (dedifferentiation path to damage-associated PT cell state) and the other toward the area with high levels of maturation-associated genes (redifferentiation path to differentiated PT cell state).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 8C.

claim: Quantitative RT-PCR analyses confirmed the transient induction of Sox9, Cdh6, and Vcam1 genes after mild ischemic injury (20 min ischemia) and persistently elevated expression after severe ischemic injury (30 min) through 21 days after injury.
source: To determine the temporal dynamics of damage-associated PT cell state in adaptive and maladaptive repair and validate the computational analyses, we performed expression analyses of multiple marker genes for this PT cell state in successful and failed renal repair processes. Quantitative RT-PCR analyses for Sox9, Cdh6, and Vcam1 genes confirmed the transient induction of these genes and resolution after mild ischemic injury (20 min ischemia, Fig, 2B), but persistently elevated expression after severe ischemic injury (30 min) through 21 days after injury (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: More VCAM1+ and Cdh6+ tubular epithelial cells were observed in IRI kidneys after 30 min than 20 min ischemia.
source: Using immunofluorescence and in situ hybridization, we observed more VCAM1+ and Cdh6+ tubular epithelial cells in IRI kidneys after 30 min than 20 min ischemia (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The number of SOX9-positive cells was similarly increased between kidneys with mild and severe IRI on day 7 compared to baseline.
source: The number of SOX9-positive cells was similarly increased between kidneys with mild and severe IRI on day 7 compared to baseline (Figure 2, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 2, D and E.

claim: SOX9 expression was reduced to baseline level in the kidneys that underwent mild injury while it persisted up to 6 months after severe IRI.
source: Notably, SOX9 expression was reduced to baseline level in the kidneys that underwent mild injury while it persisted up to 6 months after severe IRI (Figure 2, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 2, D and E.

claim: Clusters of SOX9+VCAM1+ cells were observed in the remaining parenchyma at 6 months post-severe IRI, but not in the post mild-IRI kidneys.
source: We observed clusters of SOX9+VCAM1+ cells in the remaining parenchyma at 6 months post-severe IRI, but not in the post mild-IRI kidneys (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, B and C.

claim: Severe IRI injury is associated with a reduction of homeostatic gene expressions (Acsm2 and Slc34a1) and the number of fully differentiated PT cells.
source: In accordance with the hypothesis that severe IRI injury is associated with increased signature of damage-associated PT cell state, there was a reduction of homeostatic gene expressions (Acsm2 and Slc34a1) and the number of fully differentiated PT cells, which have high lotus tetragonolobus lectin (LTL)-binding (Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 6, B-D), (Marable et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6, B-D, and citation to published literature (Marable et al., 2020).

claim: Low expression of ACSM2B, the human ortholog of Acsm2, is correlated with reduced renal function in patients with CKD.
source: This finding is in line with a clinical correlation between low expression of ACSM2B, the human ortholog of Acsm2, and reduced renal function in patients with CKD (Ledo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ledo et al., 2015).

claim: Severe ischemia (30 min) induces more robust accumulation of Sox9-lineage-labeled cells than mild ischemic injury (20 min) in the cortex and outer medulla of the IRI-kidneys on day 21.
source: To further characterize the dynamic changes and plasticity of proximal tubular cell state, we employed a CreERT2 allele of Sox9, a highly enriched gene in the damage-associated PT cell state (DA-PT, Figure 1—figure supplement 5C), combined with Rosa26tdTomato reporter to carry out lineage tracing (Figure 3A). In this mouse line (Sox9IRES-CreERT2; Rosa26tdTomato), tamoxifen administration permanently labels the Sox9-lineage cells with the tdTomato fluorescent reporter and provides the spatial information of the cells with a history of Sox9 expression. On day 21, we found that severe ischemia (30 min) induces more robust accumulation of Sox9-lineage-labeled cells than mild ischemic injury (20 min) in the cortex and outer medulla of the IRI-kidneys (Figure 3, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3, B and C.

claim: Approximately 25% of Sox9-lineage cells that underwent severe IRI were positive for VCAM1 on day 21, suggesting that part of Sox9-lineage cells did not fully redifferentiate after severe injury.
source: Approximately 25% percent of Sox9-lineage cells that underwent severe IRI were positive for VCAM1 on day 21, suggesting that part of Sox9-lineage cells did not fully redifferentiate after severe injury (Figure 3, D and E; 30 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 3, D and E. The suggestion about redifferentiation is an inference from the data.

claim: Only a few Sox9-lineage cells that underwent mild injury were VCAM1 positive on day 21, indicating successful redifferentiation.
source: In contrast, only a few Sox9-lineage cells that underwent mild injury were VCAM1 positive at this time, indicating successful redifferentiation (Figure 3, D and E; 20 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 3, D and E. The indication about redifferentiation is an inference from the data.

claim: Loss of plasticity and impaired redifferentiation of damage-associated PT cells underlie the failed renal repair/regeneration process.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that loss of plasticity and impaired redifferentiation of damage-associated PT cells underlie the failed renal repair/regeneration process (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3 and other data in the manuscript.

claim: NicheNet predicted ligand-receptor pairs in which ligands from damage-associated PT cells interact with receptors in monocytes or macrophages.
source: To determine the intercellular interactions between damage-associated PT cells and myeloid cells, we used NicheNet, a computational algorithm tool that infers ligand-receptor interactions and downstream target genes (Figure 4, A-D), (Browaeys et al., 2020). We applied NicheNet to predict ligand-receptor pairs in which ligands from damage-associated PT cells interact with receptors in monocyte or macrophages (Figure 4, A and C), (Browaeys et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis using NicheNet shown in Figure 4, A-D, and citation to the method (Browaeys et al., 2020).

claim: Among the top five predicted ligands expressed in damage-associated PT cells, enrichment of Icam1, Pdgfb, and Apoe expression was confirmed in this cell state.
source: Among the top five predicted ligands expressed in damage-associated PT cells, we confirmed the enrichment of Icam1, Pdgfb, and Apoe expression in this cell state (Figure 4E, arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Icam1 and Pdgfb have been implicated in human AKI.
source: Icam1 and Pdgfb have been implicated in human AKI (Famulski et al., 2012), and Apoe genetic variation has been linked with CKD progression (Hsu et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Famulski et al., 2012).

claim: Apoe genetic variation has been linked with CKD progression.
source: Icam1 and Pdgfb have been implicated in human AKI (Famulski et al., 2012), and Apoe genetic variation has been linked with CKD progression (Hsu et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hsu et al., 2005).

claim: mRNA expression of Icam1, Pdgfb, and Apoe were markedly increased in the kidneys showing the accumulation of damage-associated PT cells compared to post-IRI kidneys without the accumulation.
source: As inferred by NicheNet, mRNA expression of Icam1, Pdgfb, and Apoe were markedly increased in the kidneys showing the accumulation of damage-associated PT cells compared to post-IRI kidneys without the accumulation (Figure 4F; 30 min vs. 20 min ischemia).
evidence: This claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Genes associated with glutathione metabolic processes and anti-oxidative stress response pathways are overrepresented in the differentiated mouse PT cell cluster.
source: Next, we investigated the molecular mechanisms that are critical for cells to traverse between differentiated PT cells and damage-associated PT cells. To this end, we analyzed the transcriptional signature of PT cells in the differentiated/mature cluster to identify critical pathways to maintain this cellular state. We found that genes associated with glutathione metabolic processes and anti-oxidative stress response pathways are overrepresented in the differentiated mouse PT cell cluster (Figure 5A; Figure 1—figure supplement 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analyses shown in Figure 5A; Figure 1—figure supplement 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glutathione metabolic processes and anti-oxidative stress response pathways are enriched in normal differentiated human PT cells.
source: We also found that these pathways are enriched in normal differentiated human PT cells (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2, A and B; GSE131882).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analyses of human kidney data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2, A and B.

claim: Oxidative stress-induced signaling pathways related to failed renal repair, such as cellular senescence and DNA damage responses, were highly enriched in damage-associated PT cells.
source: Mirroring these findings, oxidative stress-induced signaling pathways related to failed renal repair, such as cellular senescence and DNA damage responses (Kishi et al., 2019; Canaud et al., 2019), were highly enriched in damage-associated PT cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citations to published literature (Kishi et al., 2019; Canaud et al., 2019).

claim: Glutathione-mediated anti-oxidative stress responses are critical for maintaining the cellular identity of fully differentiated PT cells.
source: Taken together, we propose that glutathione-mediated anti-oxidative stress responses are critical for maintaining the cellular identity of fully differentiated PT cells, and dysregulation of these pathways underlies the failure of damage-associated PT cells to redifferentiate into normal PT cell state.
evidence: This is a proposal/hypothesis inferred from the gene ontology enrichment analyses and other data in the manuscript.

claim: Dysregulation of glutathione-mediated anti-oxidative stress responses underlies the failure of damage-associated PT cells to redifferentiate into normal PT cell state.
source: Taken together, we propose that glutathione-mediated anti-oxidative stress responses are critical for maintaining the cellular identity of fully differentiated PT cells, and dysregulation of these pathways underlies the failure of damage-associated PT cells to redifferentiate into normal PT cell state.
evidence: This is a proposal/hypothesis inferred from the gene ontology enrichment analyses and other data in the manuscript.

claim: The genes encoding the glutathione/GPX4 defense pathway were markedly downregulated in damage-associated PT cells (DA-PT) compared to differentiated PT cells (PT).
source: To investigate whether ferroptotic stress underlies the emergence and accumulation of damage-associated PT cells in addition to its known role in inducing cell death during maladaptive repair, we first tested the expression of the canonical anti-ferroptosis defense pathway, glutathione/GPX4 axis (Figure 5B). In agreement with the underrepresentation of glutathione metabolic process in damage-associated PT cells, the genes encoding the glutathione/GPX4 defense pathway were markedly downregulated in this PT cell state (DA-PT) compared to differentiated PT cells (PT), suggesting that damage-associated PT cells are potentially vulnerable to ferroptotic stress (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Damage-associated PT cells are potentially vulnerable to ferroptotic stress.
source: In agreement with the underrepresentation of glutathione metabolic process in damage-associated PT cells, the genes encoding the glutathione/GPX4 defense pathway were markedly downregulated in this PT cell state (DA-PT) compared to differentiated PT cells (PT), suggesting that damage-associated PT cells are potentially vulnerable to ferroptotic stress (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a suggestion/inference based on the downregulation of glutathione/GPX4 pathway genes shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Significant upregulation of Acsl4 was identified in damage-associated PT cells.
source: We then analyzed the expression of ferroptotic stress biomarkers such as malondialdehyde (MDA, a lipid peroxidation product) and acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4), which also regulate cellular sensitivity to ferroptosis (Kagan et al., 2017; Doll et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2017; Kenny et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019). A recent pharmacological inhibitor study showed that ACSL4 is a reliable maker for ferroptotic stress in murine model of ischemic AKI (Zhao et al., 2020). We identified significant upregulation of Acsl4 in damage-associated PT cells in dot-plots (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5C and citations to published literature (Kagan et al., 2017; Doll et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2017; Kenny et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: ACSL4 is a reliable marker for ferroptotic stress in murine model of ischemic AKI.
source: A recent pharmacological inhibitor study showed that ACSL4 is a reliable maker for ferroptotic stress in murine model of ischemic AKI (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: Severe ischemia (30 min) induces more expression of ferroptotic stress markers (MDA and ACSL4) in SOX9+ cells than mild ischemic injury (20 min).
source: The co-expression of markers for damage-associated PT cells and ferroptotic stress was confirmed by immunofluorescence for SOX9, MDA, and ACSL4 (Figure 5, D-G). We found that severe ischemia (30 min) induces more expression of ferroptotic stress markers in SOX9+ cells than mild ischemic injury (20 min) (Figure 5, E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 5, D-G.

claim: SOX9+ damage-associated PT cells undergo high ferroptotic stress after severe ischemic injury.
source: These data demonstrate that SOX9+ damage-associated PT cells undergo high ferroptotic stress after severe ischemic injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunofluorescence data showing co-expression of SOX9 and ferroptotic stress markers.

claim: The emergence of damage-associated PT cells (SOX9+VCAM1+ cells) was observed in aristolochic acid nephropathy (AAN) and unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) models.
source: To address whether the emergence of damage-associated PT cells is specific to IRI injury or appears in other cases of acute kidney injury, we investigated the co-expression of SOX9 and VCAM1 in models of toxic renal injury (aristolochic acid nephropathy, AAN) and obstructive renal injury (unilateral ureteral obstruction, UUO), which lead to severe fibrosis. By immunofluorescence analyses of SOX9 and VCAM1 co-expression, we found the emergence of damage-associated PT cells in both models (Figure 6, A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6, A and C.

claim: SOX9-positive tubular epithelial cells in AAN and UUO models showed co-expression of ACSL4, suggesting that ferroptotic stress of damage-associated PT cells is a conserved response to kidney injury across various etiologies.
source: Furthermore, the SOX9-positive tubular epithelial cells in these models showed co-expression of ACSL4, suggesting that ferroptotic stress of damage-associated PT cells is a conserved response to kidney injury across various etiologies (Figure 6, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6, B and C. The suggestion about conserved response is an inference from the data.

claim: A cell population enriched for genes expressed in mouse damage-associated PT cells, including SOX9, VCAM1, CDH6, and VIM, was found in human AKI kidneys.
source: We then investigated whether molecularly similar damage-associated PT cells can be observed in human AKI. We analyzed scRNA-seq data from biopsy samples of two transplanted human kidneys with evidence of AKI and acute tubular injury but no evidence of rejection (GSE145927; Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), (Malone et al., 2020). We found a cell population that is enriched for genes expressed in mouse damage-associated PT cells, including SOX9, VCAM1, CDH6, and VIM. This cellular population also showed decreased expression of homeostatic PT genes (ALDOB, MIOX, and GPX4) (Figure 6, State 3; D, and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of human single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6D and E, and citation to the data source (Malone et al., 2020).

claim: Trajectory inference suggests that damage-associated PT cells emerge from mature differentiated PT cells with high expression of homeostatic genes in human kidneys.
source: Trajectory inference using Monocle 3 suggests that damage-associated PT cells emerge from mature differentiated PT cells with high expression of homeostatic genes in human kidneys (PT to DA-PT-like in Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory inference analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The glutathione metabolic gene signature is high in mature PT cells and decreases along the trajectory to DA-PT-like cells in human kidneys.
source: Interestingly, the glutathione metabolic gene signature is high in mature PT cells and decreases along the trajectory to DA-PT-like cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of human single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The emergence of damage-associated PT cells is a mechanism of acute kidney injury and repair that is shared by humans and mice.
source: These data suggest that the emergence of damage-associated PT cells is a mechanism of acute kidney injury and repair that is shared by humans and mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the analysis of human and mouse single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Genetic deletion of Gpx4 in Sox9-lineage cells was successfully confirmed by immunofluorescence.
source: To test this hypothesis, we generated a mouse model that selectively and conditionally deletes Gpx4 in Sox9-lineage cells (Sox9IRES-CreERT2; Gpx4flox/flox, hereafter conditional knockout [cKO]; Figure 7A). Genetic deletion of Gpx4 robustly induces ferroptotic stress and triggers ferroptosis (Yang et al., 2014; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014). In this mouse line, exons 4–7 of the Gpx4 allele, which include the catalytically active selenocysteine site of the GPX4 protein, is deleted in a tamoxifen-inducible manner selectively in Sox9-lineage cells. We subjected the cKO mice and littermate control mice to mild renal ischemic stress (ischemic time 22 min). This condition induces robust Sox9-CreERT2 expression but does not induce the failed renal repair phenotype in control mice (Gpx4 flox/flox). We induced Gpx4 deletion at the time of injury by tamoxifen injection (Figure 7A). The littermate control mice were subjected to the same renal ischemic stress and tamoxifen. We confirmed successful deletion of GPX4 protein by immunofluorescence (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, B and C) and found that expression of the ferroptotic stress marker ACSL4 was increased on day 21 post-IRI in cKO kidneys compared to littermate kidneys that underwent the same ischemic stress (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1, B and C.

claim: Expression of the ferroptotic stress marker ACSL4 was increased on day 21 post-IRI in cKO kidneys compared to littermate kidneys that underwent the same ischemic stress.
source: We confirmed successful deletion of GPX4 protein by immunofluorescence (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, B and C) and found that expression of the ferroptotic stress marker ACSL4 was increased on day 21 post-IRI in cKO kidneys compared to littermate kidneys that underwent the same ischemic stress (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1, D and E.

claim: Post-ischemic cKO kidneys were atrophic and showed severe tubular injury on histological evaluation on day 21.
source: The post-ischemic cKO kidneys were atrophic and showed severe tubular injury on histological evaluation on day 21 and exhibited marked accumulation of KIM1+KRT8+ injured tubular cells (Figure 7, B-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7, B-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Post-ischemic cKO kidneys exhibited marked accumulation of KIM1+KRT8+ injured tubular cells.
source: The post-ischemic cKO kidneys were atrophic and showed severe tubular injury on histological evaluation on day 21 and exhibited marked accumulation of KIM1+KRT8+ injured tubular cells (Figure 7, B-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7, C and D.

claim: Control littermate kidneys that underwent the same ischemic stress exhibited resolution of histological changes and fewer KIM1+KRT8+ cells.
source: By contrast, control littermate kidneys that underwent the same ischemic stress exhibited resolution of histological changes and fewer KIM1+KRT8+ cells (Figure 7, C and D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7, C and D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Post-ischemic cKO kidneys exhibited massive accumulation of F4/80+ macrophages, αSMA+ myofibroblasts, and increased collagen synthesis.
source: The post-ischemic cKO kidneys also exhibited massive accumulation of F4/80+ macrophages, αSMA+ myofibroblasts, and increased collagen synthesis (Figure 7, E-F; Figure 7—figure supplement 3, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7, E-F; Figure 7—figure supplement 3, B and C.

claim: Genetic deletion of Gpx4 led to increased TUNEL+ tubular epithelial cells in cKO kidneys.
source: Then, we assessed the number of cell death by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-mediated dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) assay, which detects ferroptotic cell death in Gpx4-deleted tissues (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014). Consistent with the known role of GPX4 to prevent ferroptosis, genetic deletion of Gpx4 led to the increased TUNEL+ tubular epithelial cells in cKO kidneys (Figure 7, G and H; See Figure 7—figure supplement 4 for CLK).
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 7, G and H, and citation to published literature (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014).

claim: Genetic induction of ferroptotic stress in Sox9-lineage cells is sufficient to prevent normal renal repair after mild ischemic injury and to mimic the failed renal repair phenotype observed after severe ischemic injury.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that genetic induction of ferroptotic stress in Sox9-lineage cells is sufficient to prevent normal renal repair after mild ischemic injury and to mimic the failed renal repair phenotype observed after severe ischemic injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from the Gpx4 conditional knockout experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Increased numbers of VCAM1+EMCN–F4/80– cells (damage-associated PT cells) were observed in post-ischemic cKO kidneys on day 21.
source: We then investigated if the number of damage-associated PT cells was increased in the Gpx4 cKO kidneys after mild ischemic injury. While VCAM1 is strongly induced in damage-associated PT cells and serves as a reliable marker, it is also expressed weakly in F4/80+ macrophages and endomucin (EMCN)+ endothelial cells after kidney injury (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A; see UMAP). For the precise quantification of damage-associated PT cells, we co-stained the kidneys with VCAM1, EMCN, and F4/80, and scored VCAM1+F4/80–EMCN– cells as damage-associated PT cells (Figure 8, B and C; and Figure 7—figure supplement 3D). Supporting our hypothesis, we observed increased numbers of VCAM1+EMCN–F4/80– cells in post-ischemic cKO kidneys on day 21, while the value was at a baseline level in control littermate kidneys that underwent the same mild ischemic stress (Figure 8, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 8, B and C.

claim: Confocal imaging identified the colocalization of tdTomato (Sox9-lineage) and VCAM1 and ACSL4 in the post-IRI cKO kidneys.
source: We further employed a genetic fate-mapping strategy in Gpx4-deficient Sox9-lineage cells by generating a mouse line that harbors Sox9IRES-CreERT2; Gpx4flox/flox; Rosa26tdTomato alleles. Confocal imaging identified the colocalization of tdTomato (Sox9-lineage) and VCAM1 and ACSL4 in the post-IRI cKO kidneys (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Other molecular markers of damage-associated PT cell state, such as Cdh6 and Sox9, were increased in cKO kidneys on day 21 post-IRI.
source: Other molecular markers of damage-associated PT cell state, such as Cdh6 and Sox9, were also increased in cKO kidneys on day 21 post-IRI (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: VCAM1+ cells in cKO kidneys were positive for SOX9.
source: These VCAM1+ cells were also positive for SOX9 (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: In situ hybridization confirmed robust Cdh6 expression in tubular epithelial cells in post-ischemic cKO kidneys.
source: In situ hybridization confirmed robust Cdh6 expression in tubular epithelial cells in post-ischemic cKO kidneys (Figure 8G and Figure 7—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8G and Figure 7—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Ferroptotic stress drives the accumulation of damage-associated PT cells by preventing redifferentiation of these transient inflammatory epithelial cells into normal PT cell state and augments renal inflammation and fibrosis.
source: These data substantiate our model that ferroptotic stress drives the accumulation of damage-associated PT cells by preventing redifferentiation of these transient inflammatory epithelial cells into normal PT cell state and augments renal inflammation and fibrosis (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from the Gpx4 conditional knockout experiments shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Daily administration of liproxstatin-1 potently mitigated renal atrophy in cKO IRI-kidneys.
source: We next investigated whether pharmacological inhibition of ferroptosis blunts the dynamic changes seen in proximal tubular cells. We administered liproxstatin-1, an in vivo active ferroptosis inhibitor that scavenges lipid peroxides (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014), to our cKO mice that underwent mild renal ischemia (Figure 9A). The same volume of vehicle solution (1% dimethyl sulfoxide in phosphate-buffered saline) was administered to cKO and littermate controls (Gpx4flox/flox), and these animals underwent the same procedure of unilateral IRI. While vehicle-treated IRI-kidneys of control genotype did not show renal atrophy, cKO IRI-kidneys with daily vehicle injections exhibited renal atrophy (Figure 9B). We further confirmed effective genetic targeting in our cKO IRI-kidneys from the vehicle and liproxstatin-1-treated groups by using tdTomato-lineage tracing and GPX4 immunohistochemistry (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, B and C). Daily administration of liproxstatin-1 potently mitigated the renal atrophy and reduced expression of renal tubular injury markers in cKO IRI-kidneys (KIM1 and KRT8; Figure 9, B-D; Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the liproxstatin-1 treatment experiment shown in Figure 9, B-D.

claim: Daily administration of liproxstatin-1 reduced expression of renal tubular injury markers (KIM1 and KRT8) in cKO IRI-kidneys.
source: Daily administration of liproxstatin-1 potently mitigated the renal atrophy and reduced expression of renal tubular injury markers in cKO IRI-kidneys (KIM1 and KRT8; Figure 9, B-D; Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9, C and D; Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Liproxstatin-1 prevented the accumulation of SOX9+VCAM1+ proximal tubular cells.
source: Notably, liproxstatin-1 prevented the accumulation of SOX9+VCAM1+ proximal tubular cells (Figure 9, E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 9, E and F.

claim: Liproxstatin-1 reduced the expression of Sox9, Vcam1, and Cdh6 (DA-PT markers) to the same level as in contralateral uninjured kidneys.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR analyses confirmed that the expression of Sox9, Vcam1, and Cdh6 (DA-PT markers) were all reduced by liproxstatin-1 to the same level as in contralateral uninjured kidneys (Figure 9G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: TUNEL staining showed a significant reduction of TUNEL+ cells in the liproxstatin-1-treated IRI-cKO kidneys compared to the vehicle-treated IRI-cKO kidneys.
source: Moreover, TUNEL staining showed a significant reduction of TUNEL+ cells in the liproxstatin-1-treated IRI-cKO kidneys compared to the vehicle-treated IRI-cKO kidneys (Figure 9, H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 9, H and I.

claim: Liproxstatin-1 potently ameliorated the pathologic changes of proximal tubular cells and overall damage of Gpx4-deficient kidneys that underwent IRI.
source: Collectively, liproxstatin-1 potently ameliorated the pathologic changes of proximal tubular cells and overall damage of Gpx4-deficient kidneys that underwent IRI (Figure 9J).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from the liproxstatin-1 treatment experiment shown in Figure 9.

claim: The study broadens the roles of ferroptotic stress from being restricted to the induction of regulated cell death (ferroptosis) to include the promotion and accumulation of a pathologic cell state.
source: In summary, our study broadens the roles of ferroptotic stress from one that is restricted to the induction of regulated cell death (ferroptosis) to include the promotion and accumulation of a pathologic cell state, processes that underlie maladaptive repair.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GPX4 is a key coordinator of proximal tubular cell fate for renal repair and regeneration by preventing both cell death and cell death-independent pathologic changes after IRI.
source: Our data collectively advances our understanding of the ferroptotic cell death pathway by identifying a novel role of ferroptotic stress in promoting and accumulating pathologic cellular state beyond its known role to trigger non-apoptotic regulated cell death (ferroptosis). GPX4 is a key coordinator of proximal tubular cell fate for renal repair and regeneration by preventing both cell death and cell death-independent pathologic changes after IRI.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the manuscript, particularly the Gpx4 deletion and liproxstatin-1 treatment experiments.
